planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in part shade; Sierra laurel is a western montane bog native that needs cool, wet roots and struggles in typical garden heat unless sited carefully.

directions: Sierra laurel is a stiffly upright evergreen shrub native to boggy meadows, springs, and streambanks of the Sierra Nevada and Klamath Mountains at mid-to-high elevation, distinguishing it from its lowland eastern relatives by its tolerance for cold, saturated, mucky ground. Glossy, leathery, oval leaves clothe upright stems, and in late spring erect terminal racemes of small white, fragrant, urn-shaped flowers stand above the foliage rather than dangling beneath it as in most other leucothoes. Plant in a permanently moist to boggy, acidic site such as a pond margin or seep, where it tolerates more sun than other leucothoes provided the roots never dry out. Best suited to cool-summer mountain and coastal gardens; it resents hot, dry conditions and heavy clay that puddles then bakes.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; 'Nana' is a true dwarf sport that keeps the species' arching habit on a fraction of the footprint, useful where full-size leucothoe would quickly outgrow the bed.

directions: 'Nana' is a compact, slow-growing selection of native drooping leucothoe, reaching only about two to three feet tall while spreading considerably wider on the same gracefully arching, layered stems as the species. Glossy dark green summer foliage turns deep burgundy-purple in cold weather, and small, fragrant, white, urn-shaped flowers hang in short racemes beneath the branches in May. Its reduced height makes it far easier to tuck into foundation plantings, small woodland borders, or beneath windows than standard drooping leucothoe, without sacrificing the fine winter color or elegant form. Grow in consistently moist, strongly acidic soil in shade to part shade, sheltered from winter wind and harsh afternoon sun.

common_name: Red Lips Leucothoe (Dark Purple Dwarf Coast Doghobble)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Red Lips arose as a natural branch mutation on 'Scarletta' and stays noticeably smaller and darker than its parent.

directions: Red Lips is a patented sport discovered in a planting of 'Scarletta' leucothoe, distinguished by its noticeably smaller, narrower leaves and much darker, glossy purple-black winter foliage held on a compact, dense mound. New spring growth emerges bright red before maturing to deep green through summer, then shifts into its signature near-black purple through fall and winter. Small, white, urn-shaped flowers dangle beneath the arching stems in late spring, typical of the genus. Grow in consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil in part shade, protected from hot afternoon sun and drying winter wind, which can scorch the foliage; its compact habit suits smaller foundation beds better than full-size axillaris selections.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; ReJoyce was selected as a found seedling for its strong wine-red and orange color cycling and good heat tolerance.

directions: ReJoyce is a compact, arching selection of native coastal doghobble discovered as a chance seedling in a New Jersey nursery, prized for foliage that cycles through wine-red and orange in cool weather before greening up through summer and cycling back to wine-red and orange again each fall. Delicate, urn-shaped white flowers dangle from the arching stems in spring and draw early pollinators. The plant shows good tolerance of both summer heat and winter cold for the genus, along with resistance to the leaf-spot fungal issues that sometimes trouble older leucothoe cultivars. Grow in average to consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; its dense, mounding habit works well as a low informal hedge or foundation planting in woodland-edge gardens.
